title: What We Can Do for the Environment
writingModel: The Environment: What Students Can Do — by Zhibek Bekova

The environment is under serious threat. Temperatures have been rising for decades, biodiversity is being lost at an alarming rate, and many of the systems that support life on Earth are being pushed beyond their natural limits. This is not a future problem. It is the defining condition of the present. And students — who will live the consequences of the decisions being made now — have both a right and a responsibility to respond.

The most important thing that can be done at the individual level is to understand the problem. Environmental issues are complex, interconnected, and politically charged. Before action, knowledge is needed. Read the science. Follow organisations that are doing serious environmental work in Kazakhstan — there are several. Learn to distinguish between evidence-based information and misinformation, which is sometimes spread deliberately by industries that stand to lose from environmental regulation.

At the practical level, several things can be done in daily student life. The amount of meat consumed can be reduced — livestock farming is responsible for a significant share of global emissions. Public transport can be used instead of taxis or private cars. Energy can be conserved in dormitories by turning off lights, unplugging devices, and using cold water for washing. These are small acts, but if they are adopted widely, their collective impact is not small.

At the community level, environmental issues can be raised in student organisations, faculty bodies, and local government. The right to a clean environment is guaranteed under Kazakhstani law. If that right is being violated — if a river is being polluted, if air quality is not being monitored — it can be reported. Petitions can be signed. Officials can be contacted. Journalism can be supported.

At the deepest level, what is needed is a shift in how we think about our relationship with the natural world. The environment is not something that exists separately from us — something to be protected at a distance. It is the system we are embedded in. When rivers are damaged, communities are damaged. When species are lost, ecosystems are weakened. When air is polluted, health is affected. Everything is connected.

I am an ecology student at WKU. The Ural River runs behind my dormitory. Every morning I walk past it. Some mornings I notice that it is clear. Other mornings, I notice something that concerns me — a colour, a smell, a patch of foam. I have started noting these things down. Data can be collected by anyone. Problems can be reported by anyone. Change can be made by many people doing small things consistently, over time.
